'''''Ficus aurea''''', commonly known as the '''Florida strangler fig''' (or simply '''strangler fig'''), '''golden fig''', or '''''higuerón''''',<ref name = Harvey1998/> is a tree in the family [[Moraceae]] that is native to the U.S. state of [[Florida]], the northern and western [[Caribbean]], southern [[Mexico]] and [[Central America]] south to [[Panama]].<ref name = Berg2007>{{cite journal | last = Berg | first = C.C. | year = 2007 | title = Proposals for treating four species complexes in ''Ficus'' subgenus ''Urostigma'' section ''Americanae'' (Moraceae) | journal = Blumea | volume = 52 | issue = 2 | pages = 295–312 | doi = 10.3767/000651907X609034  | doi-access = free| bibcode = 2007Blume..52..295B | url = http://www.repository.naturalis.nl/document/565073 }}</ref> The specific epithet ''aurea'' was applied by English botanist [[Thomas Nuttall]] who described the species in 1846.

''Ficus aurea'' is a [[strangler fig]]. In [[Ficus|fig]]s of this group, seed germination usually takes place in the canopy of a [[host (biology)|host]] tree with the seedling living as an [[epiphyte]] until its roots establish contact with the ground. After that, it enlarges and strangles its host, eventually becoming a free-standing tree in its own right. Individuals may reach {{convert|30|m|ft|-1|abbr=on}} in height. The tree provides habitat, food and shelter for a host of tropical lifeforms including epiphytes in [[cloud forests]] and [[bird]]s, [[mammal]]s, [[reptile]]s and [[invertebrate]]s. ''F. aurea'' is used in [[traditional medicine]], for [[Hedge|live fencing]], as an [[Ornamental plant|ornamental]] and as a [[bonsai]].

==Description==
[[File:Ficus aurea01.jpg|thumb|left|200px|''Ficus aurea'' sapling showing elliptic leaf shape at [[Long Key]], [[Florida]]]]
''Ficus aurea'' is a tree which may reach heights of {{convert|30|m|ft|0|abbr=on}}.<ref>[https://www.tropicos.org/Name/21300459?projectid=7 Flora de Nicaragua] database. Tropicos. {{in lang|es}} Retrieved on 2008-07-02</ref> It is [[Plant sexuality|monoecious]]: each tree bears functional male and female flowers.<ref name=B&P1992a/> The size and shape of the leaves is variable. Some plants have leaves that are usually less than 10 cm (4 in) long while others have leaves that are larger. The [[Leaf shape|shape of the leaves]] and of the [[Leaf#Base of the leaf|leaf base]] also varies—some plants have leaves that are oblong or elliptic with a wedge-shaped to rounded base, while others have heart-shaped or ovate leaves with [[Cordate (leaf shape)|cordate]] to rounded bases. ''F. aurea'' has paired figs<ref name = Berg2007/> which are green when unripe, turning yellow as they ripen.<ref name = IFAS>{{cite web |last=Gilman |first=Edward F. |author2=Watson, Dennis G. |date=December 2006 |title=''Ficus aurea'': Strangler Fig |publisher=Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (ENH409) |url=http://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/ST250 |access-date=2008-06-10}}</ref> They differ in size (0.6–0.8 cm [0.2–0.3 in], about 1 cm [0.4 in], or 1.0–1.2 cm [0.4–0.5 in] in diameter); figs are generally [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]], but in parts of northern [[Mesoamerica]] figs are borne on short stalks known as [[peduncle (botany)|peduncles]].<ref name = Berg2007/>

==Taxonomy==
With about 750 species, ''[[Ficus]]'' ([[Moraceae]]) is one of the largest [[angiosperm]] genera (David Frodin of [[Chelsea Physic Garden]] ranked it as the 31st largest genus).<ref name = Frodin1994>{{cite journal | last = Frodin | first = David G. | year = 2004| title = History and concepts of big plant genera | journal = Taxon | volume = 53 | issue = 3 | pages = 753–776 | doi = 10.2307/4135449 | jstor = 4135449 | bibcode = 2004Taxon..53..753F }}</ref> ''Ficus aurea'' is classified in the [[subgenus]] ''Urostigma'' (the strangler figs) and the [[section (botany)|section]] ''Americana''.<ref name = Berg2007/> Recent molecular [[Phylogenetics|phylogenies]] have shown that subgenus ''Urostigma'' is [[polyphyletic]], but have strongly supported the validity of section ''Americana'' as a [[clade|discrete group]] (although its exact relationship to section ''Galoglychia'' is unclear).<ref name="Rønsted">{{cite journal | last = Rønsted | first = N. | author2 = Weiblen, G. D.| author3 = Clement, W. L.| author4 = Zerega, N. J. C.|author5-link=Vincent Savolainen| author5 = Savolainen, V. | year = 2008 | title = Reconstructing the phylogeny of figs (Ficus, Moraceae) to reveal the history of the fig pollination mutualism | journal = Symbiosis | volume = 45 | issue = 1–3 | pages = 45–56 | url = http://geo.cbs.umn.edu/RonstedEtAl2008a.pdf }}</ref>

[[File:Ficusindicamaxima.jpg|thumb|left|Engraving of ''Ficus maxima indica'' after a drawing by Hans Sloane, published 1725, the earliest published illustration of ''Ficus aurea'' and the basis of Thomas Miller's ''[[Ficus maxima]]''. The unpaired figs in the illustration led to confusion as to the identity of the species described by Miller.]]
[[Thomas Nuttall]] described the species in the second volume of his 1846 work ''The North American Sylva''<ref name = Berg2003/> with specific epithet ''aurea'' ('golden' in [[Latin]]).<ref>{{cite book|author = Simpson DP| title = Cassell's Latin Dictionary | publisher = Cassell Ltd.| year = 1979|edition = 5th|location = London|page = 883| isbn=978-0-304-52257-6}}</ref> In 1768, Scottish botanist [[Philip Miller]] described ''[[Ficus maxima]]'', citing [[Carl Linnaeus]]' ''[[Hortus Cliffortianus]]'' (1738) and [[Hans Sloane]]'s ''Catalogus plantarum quæ in insula Jamaica'' (1696). Sloane's illustration of the species, published in 1725, depicted it with figs borne singly, a characteristic of the ''Ficus'' subgenus ''[[Pharmacosycea]]''.<ref>{{cite book| last =Sloane | first =Hans | author-link = Hans Sloane | title =A voyage to the islands Madera, Barbados, Nieves, S. Christophers and Jamaica | publisher =B.M | year =1725 }}</ref> As a member of the subgenus ''[[Urostigma]]'', ''F. aurea'' has paired figs. However, a closer examination of Sloane's description led Cornelis Berg to conclude that the illustration depicted a member of the subgenus ''Urostigma'' (since it had other diagnostic of that subgenus), almost certainly ''F. aurea'', and that the illustration of singly borne figs was probably [[artistic license]]. Berg located the plant collection upon which Sloane's illustration was based and concluded that Miller's ''F. maxima'' was, in fact, ''F. aurea''.<ref name = Berg2003>{{cite journal | last = Berg | first = Cornelis C. |date=May 2003 | title = (1587–1590) Proposals to conserve the names ''Ficus citrifolia'' against ''F. caribaea'', ''F. maxima'' with a conserved type, ''F. aurea'' against ''F. ciliolosa'', and ''F. americana'' against ''F. perforata'' (Moraceae) | journal = Taxon | volume = 52 | issue = 2 | pages = 368–370 | doi = 10.2307/3647421 | jstor = 3647421 | bibcode = 2003Taxon..52..368B | doi-access = free }}</ref> In his description of ''F. aurea'', which was based on plant material collected in Florida, Thomas Nuttall considered the possibility that his plants belonged to the species that Sloane had described, but came to the conclusion that it was a new species.<ref name = Berg2003/> Under the rules of [[botanical nomenclature]], the name ''F. maxima'' has priority over ''F. aurea'' since Miller's description was published in 1768, while Nuttall's description was published in 1846.

In their 1914 ''Flora of Jamaica'', [[William Fawcett (botanist)|William Fawcett]] and [[Alfred Barton Rendle]] linked Sloane's illustration to the tree species that was then known as ''Ficus suffocans'', a name that had been assigned to it in [[August Grisebach]]'s ''Flora of the British West Indian Islands''.<ref name = Griseb>{{cite book|last=Grisebach|first=August |author-link=August Grisebach|title=Flora of the British West Indian Islands|url=http://www.botanicus.org/bibliography/b11788513|access-date=2008-07-02|volume=1|publisher=L. Reeve & Co|location=London|year=1859}}</ref> Gordon DeWolf agreed with their conclusion and used the name ''F. maxima'' for that species in the 1960 ''Flora of Panama''.<ref name=DeWolf>DeWolf, Gordon P., Jr. "Ficus (Tourn.) L." in {{cite journal|author=Nevling, Lorin I. Jr. |year=1960 |jstor=2394704 |title=Flora of Panama. Part IV. Fascicle II|journal=Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden|volume=47|issue=2|pages=81–203|doi=10.2307/2394704 |bibcode=1960AnMBG..47...81N }}</ref> Since this use has become widespread, Berg proposed that the name ''Ficus maxima'' be [[Conserved name|conserved]] in the way DeWolf had used it,<ref name = Berg2003/> a proposal that was accepted by the nomenclatural committee.<ref name = Brummitt2005>{{cite journal | last = Brummitt | first = R.K. | year = 2005 | title = Report of the Committee for Spermatophyta: 56 | journal = Taxon | volume = 54 | issue = 2 | pages = 527–536 | doi = 10.2307/25065389 | jstor = 25065389| bibcode = 2005Taxon..54..527B | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Reassigning the name ''Ficus maxima'' did not leave ''F. aurea'' as the oldest name for this species, as German naturalist [[Johann Heinrich Friedrich Link]] had described ''Ficus ciliolosa'' in 1822. Berg concluded that the species Link described was actually ''F. aurea'', and since Link's description predated Nuttall's by 24 years, priority should have been given to the name ''F. ciliolosa''. Since the former name was widely used and the name ''F. ciliolosa'' had not been, Berg proposed that the name ''F. aurea'' be conserved.<ref name = Berg2003/> In response to this, the nomenclatural committee ruled that rather than conserving ''F. aurea'', that it would be better to reject ''F. ciliolosa''. Conserving ''F. aurea'' would mean that precedence would be given to that name over all others. By simply rejecting ''F. ciliolosa'', the committee left open the possibility that the name ''F. aurea'' could be supplanted by another older name, if one were to be discovered.<ref name = Brummitt2005/>

===Synonyms===
In 1920, American botanist [[Paul Carpenter Standley|Paul C. Standley]] described three new species based on collections from Panama and Costa Rica — ''[[Ficus tuerckheimii]]'', ''[[Ficus isophlebia|F. isophlebia]]'', and ''F. jimenezii''.<ref name = Standl>{{cite journal |last=Standley |first=Paul C. |author-link= Paul Carpenter Standley |year=1920 |title=The Mexican and Central American Species of Ficus |journal=Contributions from the United States National Herbarium |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=1–35 |url=http://www.botanicus.org/page/373799}}</ref> DeWolf concluded that they were all the same species,<ref name=DeWolf/> and Berg synonymised them with ''F. aurea''.<ref name = Berg2007/> These names have been used widely for Mexican and Central American populations, and continue to be used by some authors. Berg suspected that ''Ficus rzedowskiana'' Carvajal and Cuevas-Figueroa may also belong to this species, but he had not examined the original material upon which this species was based.<ref name = Berg2007/>

Berg considered ''F. aurea'' to be a species with at least four [[Polymorphism (biology)|morphs]]. "None of the morphs", he wrote, "can be related to certain habitats or altitudes."<ref name = Berg2007/> Thirty years earlier, William Burger had come to a very different conclusion with respect to ''Ficus tuerckheimii'', ''F. isophlebia'' and ''F. jimenezii'' — he rejected DeWolf's synonymisation of these three species as based on incomplete evidence. Burger noted that the three taxa occupied different habitats which could be separated in terms of rainfall and elevation.<ref name = Burger1974>{{cite journal | last= Burger |first= William C. |title= Ecological Differentiation in Some Congeneric Species of Costa Rican Flowering Plants |journal= Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden |volume= 61 |issue= 2 |pages= 297–306 |doi = 10.2307/2395057 |year = 1974 |jstor = 2395057|bibcode= 1974AnMBG..61..297B |url= https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/part/25396 }}</ref> [[Plants of the World Online]] accepts ''F. isophlebia'' and ''F. tuerckheimii'' as distinct species,<ref>{{cite POWO |id= 104580-2 |title= ''Ficus isophlebia'' Standl. |access-date= 30 August 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite POWO |id= 104749-2 |title= ''Ficus tuerckheimii'' Standl. |access-date= 30 August 2026}}</ref> and ''F. jimenezii'' as a synonym of ''F. aurea''.<ref name = powo/>

==Reproduction and growth==
Figs have an obligate [[Mutualism (biology)|mutualism]] with [[fig wasp]]s, (Agaonidae); figs are only pollinated by these wasps, and they can only reproduce in fig flowers. Generally, each fig species depends on a single species of wasp for pollination. The wasps are similarly dependent on their fig species in order to reproduce. ''Ficus aurea'' is pollinated by ''[[Pegoscapus mexicanus]]'' ([[William Harris Ashmead|Ashmead]]).<ref name = Jousselin2001>{{cite journal | last = Jousselin| first = Emmanuelle | author2 = Hossaert-Mckey, Martine| author3 = Vernet, Didier| author4 = Kjellberg, Finn | year = 2001 | title = Egg deposition patterns of fig pollinating wasps: implications for studies on the stability of the mutualism | journal = Ecological Entomology | volume = 26 | issue = 6 | pages = 602–608 | doi = 10.1046/j.1365-2311.2001.00368.x | bibcode = 2001EcoEn..26..602J | s2cid = 84012172 }}</ref>

Figs have complicated [[inflorescence]]s called [[syconium|syconia]]. Flowers are entirely contained within an enclosed structure. Their only connection with the outside is through a small pore called [[ostiole]]. [[Monoecious]] figs like ''F. aurea'' have both male and female flowers within the syconium.<ref name = Janzen1979>{{cite journal | last = Janzen | first = Daniel H. | author-link = Daniel Janzen | year = 1979 | title = How to be a fig | journal = Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics | volume = 10 | issue = 1 | pages = 13–51 | doi = 10.1146/annurev.es.10.110179.000305 | bibcode = 1979AnRES..10...13J }}</ref> Female flowers mature first. Once mature, they produce a [[Volatility (chemistry)|volatile]] chemical attractant.<ref name = Bronstein1995>{{cite journal | last = Bronstein | first = Judith L. |author2=Hossaert-McKey, Martine | year = 1995 | title = Hurricane Andrew and a Florida Fig Pollination Mutualism: Resilience of an Obligate Interaction | journal = Biotropica | volume = 27 | issue = 3 | pages = 373–381 | doi = 10.2307/2388922 | jstor = 2388922 | bibcode = 1995Biotr..27..373B }}</ref> Female wasps squeeze their way through the ostiole into the interior of the syconium. Inside the syconium, they pollinate the flowers, lay their eggs in some of them, and die. The eggs hatch and the larvae parasitise the flowers in which they were laid. After four to seven weeks (in ''F. aurea''), adult wasps emerge. Males emerge first, mate with the females, and cut exit holes through the walls of the fig. The male flowers mature around the same time as the female wasps emerge. The newly emerged female wasps actively pack their bodies with pollen from the male flowers before leaving through the exit holes the males have cut and fly off to find a syconium in which to lay their eggs. Over the next one to five days, figs ripen.<ref name = Bronstein1995/> The ripe figs are eaten by various mammals and birds which [[seed dispersal|disperse]] the seeds.

===Phenology===
Figs flower and fruit asynchronously.<ref name=B&P1992a>{{cite journal | last = Bronstein | first = Judith L. |author2=Patel, Aviva | year = 1992 | title = Causes and Consequences of Within-Tree Phenological Patterns in the Florida Strangling Fig, Ficus aurea (Moraceae) | journal = [[American Journal of Botany]] | volume = 79 | issue = 1 | pages = 41–48 | doi = 10.2307/2445195 | jstor = 2445195 }}</ref> Flowering and fruiting is staggered throughout the population. This fact is important for fig wasps—female wasps need to find a syconium in which to lay their eggs within a few days of emergence, something that would not be possible if all the trees in a population flowered and fruited at the same time. This also makes figs important food resources for [[frugivore]]s (animals that feed nearly exclusively on fruit); figs are one of the few fruit available at times of the year when fruit are scarce.

Although figs flower asynchronously as a population, in most species flowering is synchronised within an individual. Newly emerged female wasps must move away from their natal tree in order to find figs in which to lay their eggs. This is to the advantage of the fig, since it prevents [[self-pollination]].<ref name = Janzen1979/> In Florida, individual ''F. aurea'' trees flower and fruit asynchronously.<ref name=B&P1992a/> Within-tree asynchrony in flowering is likely to raise the probability of self-pollination, but it may be an adaptation that allows the species to maintain an adequate population of wasps at low population densities or in strongly seasonal climates.<ref name=B&P1992a/>

Flowering [[phenology]] in ''Ficus'' has been characterised into five phases. In most figs, phase A is followed almost immediately by phase B. However, in ''F. aurea'' immature inflorescences can remain dormant for more than nine months.<ref name=B&P1992a/>

===Growth===
''Ficus aurea'' is a fast-growing tree.<ref name = enviroscaping>{{cite web |last=Broschat |first= Timothy K. |author2=Alan W. Meerow |author3=Robert J. Black  |date=February 2007 |title=Enviroscaping to Conserve Energy: Trees for South Florida |publisher=Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (Circular EES-42) |url=http://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/EH142 |access-date=2008-06-10}}</ref> As a [[hemiepiphyte]] it [[Germination|germinates]] in the [[Canopy (forest)|canopy]] of a host tree and begins life as an [[epiphyte]] before growing roots down to the ground. ''F. aurea'' is also a [[strangler fig]] (not all hemiepiphytic figs are stranglers)—the roots [[anastomosis|fuse]] and encircle the host tree. This usually results in the death of the host, since it effectively [[girdling|girdles]] the tree. [[Arecaceae|Palms]], which lack [[secondary growth]], are not affected by this, but they can still be harmed by competition for light, water and nutrients.<ref name = Putz1989>{{cite journal | last = Putz | first = Francis E. |author2=N. Michele Holbrook | year = 1989 | title = Strangler Fig Rooting Habits and Nutrient Relations in the Llanos of Venezuela | journal = American Journal of Botany | volume = 76 | issue = 6 | pages = 781–788 | doi = 10.2307/2444534 | jstor = 2444534 }}</ref> Following [[Hurricane Andrew]] in 1992, ''F. aurea'' trees regenerated from [[Basal shoot|root suckers]] and standing trees.<ref name = Horvitz1998>{{cite journal | last = Horvitz | first = Carol C. | author2 = Pascarella, John B.| author3 = McMann, Stephen| author4 = Freedman, Andrea| author5 = Hofstetter, Ronald H. | year = 1988 | title = Functional Roles of Invasive Non-Indigenous Plants in Hurricane-Affected Subtropical Hardwood Forests | journal = Ecological Applications | volume = 8 | issue = 4 | pages = 947–974 |doi = 10.1890/1051-0761(1998)008[0947:FROINI]2.0.CO;2 | issn = 1051-0761}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Ficus aurea'' ranges from Florida, across the northern Caribbean to Mexico, and south across Central America. It is present in central and southern Florida and the [[Florida Keys]],<ref name=Little>{{cite book|first=Elbert L.|last=Little Jr.|title=Atlas of United States Trees|volume=5 (Florida)|year=1978|publisher=US Government Printing Office|lccn=79-653298|oclc=241660|entry-url=https://archive.org/details/atlasofunitedsta1361litt/page/n110/mode/1up|entry=Map 204, ''Ficus aurea''}}</ref> The Bahamas, the Caicos Islands, Hispaniola, Cuba, Jamaica, the Cayman Islands, [[Archipelago of San Andrés, Providencia and Santa Catalina|San Andrés]] (a Colombian possession in the western Caribbean),<ref name = Berg2007/> southern Mexico,<ref name=Serrato2004>{{cite journal | last = Serrato | first = Alejandra | author2 = Ibarra-Manríquez, Guillermo| author3 = Oyama, Ken |date=March 2004 | title = Biogeography and conservation of the genus ''Ficus'' (Moraceae) in Mexico | journal = [[Journal of Biogeography]] | volume = 31 | issue = 3 | pages = 475–485 | doi = 10.1046/j.0305-0270.2003.01039.x | bibcode = 2004JBiog..31..475S | s2cid = 82099604 }}</ref> Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, El Salvador, Costa Rica and Panama.<ref name = FloraMesoamericana>[http://www.tropicos.org/MobotProjects.aspx?project=flmaname&nameid=21300459 Ficus aurea Nutt.] Flora Mesoamericana: Lista Anotada. {{in lang|es}} Retrieved on 2008-07-02</ref> It grows from sea level up to 1,800 m (5,500 ft) [[above sea level]],<ref name = Berg2007/> in habitats ranging from [[Bahamian dry forests]],<ref name=Swagel/> to [[cloud forest]] in Costa Rica.<ref name=Sillett1995>{{cite journal | last = Sillett | first = Stephen C. | author2 = Gradstein, S. Rob| author3 = Griffin, Dana, III | year = 1995 | title = Bryophyte Diversity of Ficus Tree Crowns from Cloud Forest and Pasture in Costa Rica | journal = [[The Bryologist]] | volume = 98 | issue = 2 | pages = 251–260 | doi = 10.2307/3243312| jstor = 3243312 }}</ref>

''Ficus aurea'' is found in central and southern Florida as far north as [[Volusia County, Florida|Volusia County]];<ref>{{cite web |title=''Ficus aurea'': Distribution Map |url=https://florida.plantatlas.usf.edu/Plant.aspx?id=2466 |work=Atlas of Florida Vascular Plants |publisher=Institute for Systematic Botany, University of South Florid |access-date=2008-06-10 }}</ref> it is one of only two native fig species in Florida.<ref name = Bessey1908/> The species is present in a range of south Florida ecosystems, including coastal hardwood [[hammock (ecology)|hammocks]], [[Sabal palmetto|cabbage palm]] hammocks,
[[tropical hardwood hammocks]] and shrublands, temperate hardwood hammocks and shrublands<ref>{{cite web |author=Ken Rutchey |url=https://sofia.usgs.gov/publications/ofr/2006-1240/ |title=Vegetation Classification for South Florida Natural Areas |year=2006 |publisher=[[United States Geological Survey]] |access-date=2008-06-10 |display-authors=etal |archive-date=2008-05-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080512080413/http://sofia.usgs.gov/publications/ofr/2006-1240/ }} Open-File Report 2006-1240. <!--this needs to cite the specific page, otherwise it is useless as a web citation --></ref> and along watercourses.<ref name = Bronstein1995/> In The Bahamas, ''F. aurea'' is found in [[Bahamian dry forests|tropical dry forests]] on [[North Andros]],<ref name = Smith1992>{{cite journal | last = Smith | first = Inge K. |author2=Vankat, John L. | year = 1992 | title = Dry Evergreen Forest (Coppice) Communities of North Andros Island, Bahamas | journal = Bulletin of the Torrey Botanical Club | volume = 119 | issue = 2 | pages = 181–191 | doi = 10.2307/2997030 | jstor = 2997030 }}</ref> [[Great Exuma]]<ref name=Swagel/> and [[Bimini]].<ref>{{cite journal | last = Howard | first = Richard A. | year = 1950 | title = Vegetation of the Bimini Island Group: Bahamas, B. W. I | journal = Ecological Monographs | volume = 20 | issue = 4 | pages = 317–349 | doi = 10.2307/1943569 | jstor = 1943569 | bibcode = 1950EcoM...20..317H }}</ref> ''F. aurea'' occurs in 10 [[Administrative divisions of Mexico#States|states]] in Mexico, primarily in the south, but extending as far north as [[Jalisco]].<ref name=Serrato2004/> It is found in tropical deciduous forest, tropical semi-evergreen forest, tropical evergreen forest, cloud forest and in aquatic or subaquatic habitats.<ref name=Serrato2004/>

==Ecology==
[[File:Rubber, or Banyan Tree, on Banana River, Florida.jpg|thumb|right|200px|''Rubber, or Banyan Tree, on [[Banana River (Florida)|Banana River, Florida]]''—an 1893 photograph of what is now known as a Florida strangler fig]]
''Ficus aurea'' is a strangler fig—it tends to establish on a host tree which it gradually encircles and "strangles", eventually taking the place of that tree in the forest canopy. While this makes ''F. aurea'' an agent in the mortality of other trees, there is little to indicate that its choice of hosts is species specific. However, in [[Bahamian dry forests|dry forests]] on [[Great Exuma]] in The Bahamas, ''F. aurea'' establishes exclusively on [[Arecaceae|palms]], in spite of the presence of several other large trees that should provide suitable hosts. Eric Swagel and colleagues attributed this to the fact that [[humus]] accumulates on the leaf bases of these palms and provides a relatively moist [[microclimate]] in a dry environment, facilitating seedling survival.<ref name=Swagel>{{cite journal | last = Swagel | first = Eric N. | author2 = Bernhard, A. Van H.| author3 = Ellmore, George S. | year = 1997 | title = Substrate water potential constraints on germination of the strangler fig ''Ficus aurea'' (Moraceae) | journal = American Journal of Botany | volume = 84 | issue = 5 | pages = 716–722 | doi = 10.2307/2445908 | jstor = 2445908 | pmid = 21708624 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Figs are sometimes considered to be potential [[keystone species]] in communities of [[frugivore|fruit-eating animals]] because of their [[wikt:asynchrony|asynchronous]] fruiting patterns.<ref name=Terborgh1986>{{cite book|last=Terborgh|first=John|editor=Michael E. Soulé|editor-link=Michael E. Soulé|title=Conservation Biology: The Science of Scarcity and Diversity|year=1986|publisher=Sinauer Associates|location=Sunderland, Massachusetts|isbn=978-0-87893-795-0|pages=330–344|chapter=Keystone plant resources in the tropical forests}}</ref> Nathaniel Wheelwright reports that [[emerald toucanet]]s fed on unripe ''F. aurea'' fruit at times of fruit scarcity in [[Monteverde]], Costa Rica.<ref>{{cite journal | last = Wheelwright | first = Nathaniel T. | date = June 1985 | title = Competition for dispersers, and the timing of flowering and fruiting in a guild of tropical trees | journal = [[Oikos (journal)|Oikos]] | volume = 44 | pages = 465–477 | url = http://www.bowdoin.edu/faculty/n/nwheelwr/pdf/Compfordisp.pdf | doi = 10.2307/3565788 | issue = 3 | jstor = 3565788 | bibcode = 1985Oikos..44..465W | access-date = 2008-06-06 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090225142605/http://www.bowdoin.edu/faculty/n/nwheelwr/pdf/Compfordisp.pdf | archive-date = 2009-02-25 }}</ref> Wheelwright listed the species as a year-round food source for the [[resplendent quetzal]] at the same site.<ref>{{cite journal | last = Wheelwright | first = Nathaniel T. | year = 1983 | title = Fruits and the Ecology of Resplendent Quetzals | journal = [[The Auk]] | volume = 100 | issue = 2 | pages = 286–301 | url = http://sora.unm.edu/sites/default/files/journals/auk/v100n02/p0286-p0301.pdf | doi = 10.1093/auk/100.2.286 }}</ref> In the [[Florida Keys]], ''F. aurea'' is one of five fruit species that dominate the diet fed by [[white-crowned pigeon]]s to their nestlings.<ref name = Bancroft1994>{{cite journal | last = Bancroft | first = G. Thomas |author2=Reed Bowman | year = 1994 | title = Temporal Patterns in Diet of Nestling White-Crowned Pigeons: Implications for Conservation of Frugivorous Columbids | journal = The Auk | volume = 111 | issue = 4 | pages = 844–52 | url = http://sora.unm.edu/sites/default/files/journals/auk/v111n04/p0844-p0852.pdf | doi = 10.2307/4088816| jstor = 4088816 }}</ref> ''F. aurea'' is also important in the diet of mammalian frugivores—both fruit and young leaves are consumed by [[Guatemalan Black Howler|black howler monkeys]] in Belize.<ref name=Silver1999>{{cite journal | last = Silver | first = S. C. | author2 = L. E. T. Ostro | author3 = C. P. Yeager | author4 = R. Horwich | year = 1999 | title = Feeding ecology of the black howler monkey (''Alouatta pigra'') in Northern Belize | journal = American Journal of Primatology | volume = 45 | issue = 3 | pages = 263–279 | url = http://www.communityconservation.org/publications/feedeco98.pdf | pmid = 9651649 | doi = 10.1002/(SICI)1098-2345(1998)45:3<263::AID-AJP3>3.0.CO;2-U | s2cid = 22566572 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20111004072516/http://www.communityconservation.org/publications/feedeco98.pdf | archive-date = 2011-10-04 }}</ref>

The interaction between figs and [[fig wasp]]s is especially well-known (see section on [[Ficus aurea#Reproduction and growth|reproduction]], above). In addition to its pollinators (''Pegoscapus mexicanus''), ''F. aurea'' is exploited by a group of non-pollinating [[Chalcid wasp|chalcidoid wasps]] whose larvae develop in its figs. These include [[gall]]ers, [[inquiline]]s and [[kleptoparasite]]s as well as [[parasitoid]]s of both the pollinating and non-pollinating wasps.<ref name = Bronstein1999>{{cite journal | last = Bronstein | first = Judith L. | year = 1999 | title = Natural History of ''Anidarnes bicolor'' (Hymenoptera: Agaonidae), a Galler of the Florida Strangling Fig (''Ficus aurea'') | journal = Florida Entomologist | volume = 82 | issue = 3 | pages = 454–461 | doi = 10.2307/3496871 | jstor = 3496871 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

The invertebrates within ''F. aurea'' syconia in southern Florida include a pollinating wasp, ''P. mexicanus'', up to eight or more species of non-pollinating wasps, a plant-parasitic nematode transported by the pollinator, mites, and a predatory rove beetle whose adults and larvae eat fig wasps.<ref name = Nadel1992>{{cite journal | last = Nadel | first = Hannah | author2 = Frank, J. Howard| author3 = Knight, R. J. Jr. |date=March 1992 | title = Escapees and Accomplices: The Naturalization of Exotic ''Ficus'' and Their Associated Faunas in Florida | journal = Florida Entomologist | volume = 75 | issue = 1 | pages = 29–38 | doi = 10.2307/3495478 | jstor = 3495478 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
Nematodes: ''Schistonchus aureus'' (Aphelenchoididae) is a plant-parasitic nematode associated with the pollinator ''Pegoscapus mexicanus'' and syconia of  ''F. aurea''.<ref name = Decrappeo2001>{{cite journal  | last = Decrappeo |  first = N. |author2=Giblin-Davis, R. M. | year = 2001 | title = ''Schistonchus aureus'' n. sp. and ''S. laevigatus'' n. sp. (Aphelenchoididae): Associates of native Floridian ''Ficus'' spp. and their ''Pegoscapus'' pollinators (Agaonidae) |  journal = Journal of Nematology | volume = 33 |  pages =  91–103 | pmid = 19266003  | issue = 2–3  | pmc = 2638131 }}</ref> 
Mites: belonging to the family Tarsonemidae (Acarina) have been recognized in the syconia of ''F. aurea'' and ''F. citrifolia'', but they have not been identified even to genus, and their behavior is undescribed.<ref name="Nadel1992" />
Rove beetles: ''Charoxus spinifer'' is a rove beetle (Coleoptera: Staphylinidae) whose adults enter late-stage syconia of ''F. aurea'' and ''F. citrifolia''.<ref name ="  Frank1997">{{cite journal | last = Frank | first = J. H. |author2=Thomas, M. C. | year = 1997 | title = A new species of ''Charoxus'' (Coleoptera: Staphylinidae) from native figs (''Ficus'' spp.) in Florida |  journal = Journal of the New York Entomological Society | volume = 104 | pages = 70–78 }}</ref> Adults eat fig wasps; larvae develop within the syconia and prey on fig wasps, then pupate in the ground.<ref name ="  Frank2012">{{cite journal | last = Frank | first = J. H. |author2=Nadel, Hannah | year = 2012 | title = Life cycle and behaviour of Charoxus spinifer and Charoxus major (Coleoptera: Staphylinidae: Aleocharinae), predators of fig wasps (Hymenoptera: Agaonidae) | journal = Journal of Natural History | volume = 46 |  pages =  621–635 |  doi = 10.1080/00222933.2011.651641 | issue = 9–10 | bibcode = 2012JNatH..46..621F | s2cid = 84010406 }}</ref>

As a large tree, ''F. aurea'' can be an important host for [[epiphyte]]s. In Costa Rican cloud forests, where ''F. aurea'' is "the most conspicuous component" of intact forest,<ref name=Sillett1995/> trees in forest patches supported richer communities of epiphytic [[bryophyte]]s, while isolated trees supported greater [[lichen]] cover.<ref name=Sillett1995/>

[[Florida International University]] ecologist Suzanne Koptur reported the presence of [[Nectar#Extrafloral nectaries|extrafloral nectaries]] on ''F. aurea'' figs in the Florida [[Everglades]].<ref name = Koptur1992>{{cite journal | last = Koptur | first = Suzanne | year = 1992 | title = Plants with Extrafloral Nectaries and Ants in Everglades Habitats | journal = Florida Entomologist | volume = 75 | issue = 1 | pages = 38–50 | url = http://www.fiu.edu/%7Ekopturs/pubs/SK92FlaEnt.pdf | doi = 10.2307/3495479 | jstor = 3495479 | access-date = 2008-06-10 | archive-date = 2012-08-29 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120829173219/http://www2.fiu.edu/~kopturs/pubs/SK92FlaEnt.pdf }}</ref> Extrafloral nectaries are structures which produce [[nectar]] but are not associated with flowers. They are usually interpreted as defensive structure and are often produced in response to attack by insect [[herbivore]]s.<ref name = Heil2007>{{cite journal | last = Heil | first = Martin | year = 2007 | title = Indirect defence via tritrophic interactions | journal = New Phytologist | volume = 178 | issue = 1 | pages = 41–61 | doi = 10.1111/j.1469-8137.2007.02330.x | pmid = 18086230 | doi-access = free }}</ref> They attract insects, primarily [[ant]]s, which defend the nectaries, thus protecting the plant against herbivores.<ref name = Bronstein2006>{{cite journal | last = Bronstein | first = Judith L.| author2 = Alarcón, Ruben| author3 = Geber, Monica| year = 2006 | title = The evolution of plant–insect mutualisms | journal = New Phytologist | volume = 172 | issue = 3 | pages = 412–428 | doi = 10.1111/j.1469-8137.2006.01864.x | pmid = 17083673 | bibcode = 2006NewPh.172..412B| doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Uses==
''Ficus aurea'', amongst other related ''Ficus'' species, has been a source of bark for preparing ''[[amate]]'', the bark paper used for [[Maya codices|codices]] in the Mesoamerican civilizations. The oldest example dates back to 75 CE and was found in a [[Western Mexico shaft tomb tradition|shaft tomb culture]] site in Huitzilapa, [[Jalisco]] in [[Mexico]].<ref>{{cite book |author=Miller, Mary |author-link=Mary Miller (art historian) |author2=Karl Taube |author2-link=Karl Taube |year=1993 |title=The Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya |publisher=Thames and Hudson |location=London |isbn=0-500-05068-6 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/godssymbolsofa00mill }}</ref><ref>{{Cite thesis |degree=PhD |title=The endurance of Mexican amate paper: Exploring additional dimensions to the sustainable development concept |url= http://www.itc.nl/library/Papers_2003/phd_theses/lopez_binnquist.pdf |author=Rosaura Citlalli López Binnqüist |year=2003 |publisher=University of Twente, Enschede, Netherlands |access-date=April 15, 2011 |docket=9036519004 }}</ref>

The fruit of ''Ficus aurea'' is edible and was used for food by the [[Native Americans in the United States|Native Americans]] and early settlers in Florida; it is still eaten occasionally as a backyard source of native fruit. The latex was used to make a chewing gum, and aerial roots may have been used to make lashings, arrows, bowstrings and fishing lines. The fruit was used to make a rose-coloured dye.<ref name = FLEthnobot>{{cite web |last=Allen |first=Ginger M. |author2=Bond, Michael D. |author3=Main, Martin B. |date=December 2002 |title=50 Common Native Plants Important In Florida's Ethnobotanical History |publisher=[[Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences]] (Circular 1439) |url=http://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/UW152 |access-date=2008-06-10 |archive-date=2012-04-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120426161709/http://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/uw152 }}</ref> ''F. aurea'' was also used in [[traditional medicine]] in The Bahamas<ref>{{cite journal | last = Eldridge | first = Joan |date=October 1975 | title = Bush medicine in the Exumas and Long Island, Bahamas. A field study | journal = Economic Botany | volume = 29 | issue = 4 | pages = 307–332 | doi =10.1007/BF02862180 | bibcode = 1975EcBot..29..307E | s2cid = 25655586 }}</ref> and Florida.<ref name = FLEthnobot/> Allison Adonizio and colleagues screened ''F. aurea'' for anti-[[quorum sensing]] activity (as a possible means of anti-bacterial action), but found no such activity.<ref name = Adonizio2006>{{cite journal | last = Adonizio | first = Allison L. | author2 = Downum, Kelsey| author3 = Bennett, Bradley C.| author4 = Mathee, Kalai |author-link4=Kalai Mathee| year = 2006 | title = Anti-quorum sensing activity of medicinal plants in southern Florida | journal = Journal of Ethnopharmacology | volume = 105 | issue = 3 | pages = 427–435 | doi = 10.1016/j.jep.2005.11.025 | pmid = 16406418 }}</ref>

Individual ''F. aurea'' trees are common on dairy farms in La Cruz, Cañitas and [[Santa Elena, Costa Rica|Santa Elena]] in Costa Rica, since they are often spared when forest is converted to [[pasture]]. In interviews, farmers identified the species as useful for fence posts, [[Hedge|live fencing]] and firewood, and as a food species for wild birds and mammals.<ref name = Harvey1998>{{cite journal | last = Harvey | first = C. A. |author2=Haber, W. A. | year = 1998 | title = Remnant trees and the conservation of biodiversity in Costa Rican pastures | journal = Agroforestry Systems | volume = 44 | issue = 1 | pages = 37–68 | doi = 10.1023/A:1006122211692 | bibcode = 1998AgrSy..44...37H | s2cid = 23022677 }}</ref>

''Ficus aurea'' is used as an [[Ornamental plant|ornamental tree]], an [[Houseplant|indoor tree]] and as a [[bonsai]].<ref name="IFAS"/> Like other figs, it tends to invade built structures and foundations, and needs to be removed to prevent structural damage.<ref name="Nadel1992" /> Although young trees are described as "rather ornamental",<ref name = Bessey1908>{{cite journal | last = Bessey | first = Ernst A. | author-link = Ernst Bessey | year = 1908 | title = The Florida Strangling Figs | journal = Missouri Botanical Garden Annual Report | volume = 1908 | pages = 25–33 | doi = 10.2307/2400063 | jstor = 2400063 }}</ref> older trees are considered to be difficult to maintain (because of the [[adventitious roots]] that develop off branches) and are not recommended for small areas.<ref name = IFAS/> However, it was considered a useful tree for "enviroscaping" to conserve energy in south Florida, since it is "not as aggressive as many exotic fig species," although it must be given enough space.<ref name = enviroscaping/>
